clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive, caused by biallelic variants in CHST14, encoding dermatan 4-O-sulfotransferase-1, or less often in DSE, disrupting dermatan sulfate synthesis.
Presents at birth with multiple congenital contractures, characteristically adducted thumbs and talipes equinovarus.
Distinctive craniofacial features include a large or late-closing fontanelle, hypertelorism, short downslanting palpebral fissures, blue sclerae, low-set ears and a small mouth.
Progressive connective tissue fragility produces hyperextensible, easily bruised and fragile skin with atrophic scarring.
Recurrent large subcutaneous haematomas can be severe or life-threatening, and visceral or vascular rupture is reported.
Ophthalmological complications include glaucoma, high refractive errors and retinal detachment.
Progressive kyphoscoliosis, a tall slender habitus and recurrent joint dislocations develop over time.
Lifelong multisystem surveillance is required, covering cardiac, ophthalmic, skeletal and vascular systems.
reference.pathophysiology: CHST14 encodes dermatan 4-O-sulfotransferase-1, the enzyme that transfers sulfate to the dermatan sulfate glycosaminoglycan chains carried by proteoglycans such as decorin. Loss of enzyme function abolishes normal dermatan sulfate biosynthesis, so decorin bears aberrant chondroitin sulfate chains instead. Because decorin normally coats collagen fibrils and regulates their spacing and lateral assembly, this switch disorganises collagen fibril architecture throughout the extracellular matrix. The consequence is generalised connective tissue fragility affecting skin, joints, blood vessels, eyes and viscera, together with the congenital contractures and craniofacial features that define the subtype. Biallelic variants in DSE, encoding dermatan sulfate epimerase, impair the same pathway and cause a clinically similar phenotype.
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of CHST14 and DSE
Analysis of glycosaminoglycan and dermatan sulfate composition where available
Echocardiography and vascular imaging for structural and rupture risk
Comprehensive ophthalmological assessment including intraocular pressure
Spinal and skeletal imaging to monitor scoliosis and contractures
Cranial or soft-tissue imaging when a large haematoma is suspected
redFlags: A large or rapidly expanding subcutaneous haematoma
Signs of visceral or arterial rupture
Raised intraocular pressure or acute visual loss
Rapidly progressive scoliosis with respiratory compromise
reference.prognosis: The course is variable, with multisystem connective tissue fragility causing significant lifelong morbidity. Life-threatening haematomas and vascular or visceral rupture can occur, and life expectancy may be reduced in severely affected individuals.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the presentation as isolated arthrogryposis and missing the wider connective tissue disorder.
Overlooking the autosomal recessive inheritance and the recurrence risk for siblings.
Underestimating the risk of large, potentially life-threatening subcutaneous haematomas.
Failing to screen for ocular complications such as glaucoma and retinal detachment.
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists; management is supportive and directed at connective tissue fragility, contractures and bleeding risk
Physiotherapy, splinting and orthopaedic or orthotic management of congenital contractures, talipes and progressive scoliosis
Meticulous wound and skin care with careful surgical technique and tension-free closure given fragile, atrophic-scarring skin
Vigilance for large subcutaneous haematomas and vascular or visceral rupture, with prompt imaging and haemostatic or surgical management of significant bleeds
Cardiovascular surveillance with echocardiography and vascular imaging for structural anomalies and rupture risk
Regular ophthalmological review including intraocular pressure for glaucoma, high refractive errors and retinal detachment
Autosomal recessive genetic counselling for CHST14 and DSE variants, with family testing
